items.name: Phonograph
items.text: In 1877, in his laboratory at Menlo Park, Thomas Edison built a machine that could capture sound and play it back. A needle scratched the vibrations of a voice into a thin layer of tinfoil, and later into a wax cylinder. For the first time you could hear music without a musician standing in the room. The cylinders were hard to copy and sounded thin, but they turned a performance into something you could keep, sell and carry around. Brass bands, popular songs and recitations were the first music to be sold this way.
items.listen: Listen through the hiss: what is left of the music, and what is missing compared with a modern recording?

tracks.title: Meet Me in St. Louis, Louis

items.name: Saxophone
items.text: The Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax, born in Dinant, moved to Paris in 1842. There he designed a brass wind instrument with a reed and keys, like a clarinet. He was granted a patent for it in 1846. The saxophone was meant for military bands: loud enough for the open air, but more supple than a trumpet. In jazz it became a voice that could sing, scream and whisper. Coleman Hawkins made the tenor saxophone a solo instrument, and Charlie Parker played the lightning-fast lines of bebop on it. After the war the wailing sax gave rhythm and blues and early rock 'n' roll their punch.
items.listen: Three saxophones: when does it sound like a singing voice, and when like a scream?

items.name: Gramophone and 78 rpm record
items.text: Emile Berliner captured sound not on a cylinder but on a flat disc. The advantage: from a single master you could press thousands of copies. Around 1925, 78 revolutions per minute became the standard speed. One side of such a shellac record holds about three minutes of music, and for decades that length decided how long a pop song lasts. The record turned music into a mass product. Through gramophone records, jazz and blues reached an audience that had never seen the musicians live.
items.listen: Pay attention to the length: does the song fit into about three minutes, and can you hear that the musicians were counting on it?

items.name: Tin Pan Alley sheet music
items.who: Music publishers such as M. Witmark & Sons
items.text: Before the gramophone became commonplace, you bought a song on paper. Many middle-class families had a piano in the living room and played the latest hits themselves. From the 1880s onwards, music publishers set up shop in Manhattan, and by 1900 most of them were on West 28th Street. So much piano clatter poured out of the open windows that the street was nicknamed Tin Pan Alley, the alley of tin pans. Publishers employed staff songwriters and paid pianists to demonstrate new songs in shops and theatres. After the Ball by Charles K. Harris, from 1892, became one of the biggest hits.
items.listen: These songs were sold mainly as sheet music: are they easy to sing along to and to play at home on a piano?

items.name: Pianola and piano roll
items.text: In 1895, in Detroit, Edwin Votey built a device that made a piano play by itself. A roll of paper punched with holes ran past a row of openings; wherever air could pass through a hole, a key went down. The Aeolian Company put the Pianola on the market in 1898. People who could not play the piano could now still hear the latest ragtime at home. In the 1920s the player piano was an ordinary piece of furniture in America, and Scott Joplin and George Gershwin recorded rolls themselves. Later Conlon Nancarrow wrote music so fast and complex that only a player piano can play it.
items.listen: No pianist is playing here, but a roll of paper: can you hear that in the rhythm or in the touch?

items.name: Electrical recording and the microphone
items.text: Until 1925 musicians sang into a large horn, which scratched the vibrations directly into the record. Anyone who played softly did not get recorded. Western Electric developed a system with an electric microphone and an amplifier, and the record companies Victor and Columbia adopted it in 1925. From then on recordings sounded fuller and clearer, with low notes and quiet details. Singers could stand close to the microphone and sing intimately. That way of singing is called crooning, and it became the sound of 1930s popular music.
items.listen: The singer does not need to shout: can you hear how soft and close the voice sounds?

tracks.title: Where the Blue of the Night (Meets the Gold of the Day)

items.name: Drum kit with foot pedal
items.who: William F. Ludwig and Theobald Ludwig
items.text: Around 1900 an orchestra often had several percussionists: one for the bass drum, one for the snare drum and the cymbals. William F. Ludwig played in circus and theatre orchestras in Chicago and found the wooden pedals of his day too slow for ragtime. In 1909 he was granted a patent on a pedal with a spring that bounces back by itself after every stroke. With his brother Theobald he started a drum company. Now one musician played the bass drum with his foot and everything else with his hands. That is how the drum kit was born. In the swing era, Chick Webb and Gene Krupa turned it into an instrument for spectacular solos.
items.listen: Listen to the bass drum: can you hear the drummer's foot, and what are his hands doing at the same time?

items.name: Radio
items.text: In November 1920 the station KDKA in Pittsburgh began regular broadcasts; in The Hague, Hanso Idzerda had already been broadcasting music in 1919. During the 1920s a radio set arrived in millions of living rooms. Suddenly music was free and could be heard everywhere at once. Big bands played live on the radio and so became known across the country, and programmes such as the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville turned rural music into a national genre. Whoever got on the radio could reach an entire country in a single evening.
items.listen: Imagine hearing this from a little box in the living room: which instrument comes across best through a small loudspeaker?

items.name: Jukebox
items.text: In 1927 AMI put a coin-operated machine on the market that was electrically amplified and could choose from ten records. In the 1930s and 1940s such jukeboxes stood in cafés, roadside diners and bars all over America. For a few cents the public chose what was played. As a result, record companies knew exactly which songs were catching on, and from the 1940s Billboard kept separate jukebox charts. Fast, danceable records by jump blues bands such as Louis Jordan's were played to death in Black neighbourhoods.
items.listen: Why would this song work well in a noisy café with a coin-operated machine in the corner?

items.name: Magnetic tape
items.text: At the radio exhibition in Berlin in 1935, AEG showed the Magnetophon, a recorder that captured sound on a tape with a magnetic coating made by BASF. After the war the American company Ampex copied the technology; the Ampex 200 came on the market in 1948. Tape was a revolution: you could cut a recording, splice it, play it backwards and record over it. Composers in Paris and Cologne used it to make new music out of sounds and tape loops. Pop studios used tape to join the best sections of different takes together.
items.listen: Here the tape itself is the instrument: which sounds come from cutting, speeding up or recording one layer over another?

items.name: Plate reverb (EMT 140)
items.who: EMT (Wilhelm Franz), based on a design by Walter Kuhl
items.text: Reverb is the sound that still hangs in a hall after a note has been played. Studios created reverb with a separate echo chamber, but such a room takes up space and always sounds the same. In 1957 the German company EMT in Lahr released the EMT 140: a thin steel plate of roughly one by two metres, suspended in a wooden cabinet. A transducer makes the plate vibrate and pickups capture the reverb. With a damper you make the reverb shorter or longer. At RCA Studio B in Nashville, engineer Bill Porter used such a plate to give the voices of Roy Orbison, the Everly Brothers and Elvis Presley a bright sheen.
items.listen: Listen to the voice at the end of a line: how long does it keep ringing, and does that sound like a real hall?

items.name: Long-playing record (LP)
items.text: In 1948 Columbia introduced the long-playing record: a vinyl disc with finer grooves that turns at 33⅓ revolutions per minute. One side held more than twenty minutes of music instead of three. At first the LP was intended mainly for classical music, but jazz musicians used the space for long improvisations and singers such as Frank Sinatra made albums built around a single mood. In the 1960s the album became an art form in rock: a coherent whole with a sleeve, a running order and sometimes a concept.
items.listen: This song was made for an album: what would be lost if you heard it on its own on the radio?

tracks.title: In the Wee Small Hours of the Morning

items.name: Stereo
items.text: As early as 1931 the British engineer Alan Blumlein applied for a patent on a way of recording sound on two channels, so that you can hear where an instrument is placed. It only became a product after the LP. Westrex developed a groove that carries two channels at once. At the end of 1957 the label Audio Fidelity in New York pressed the first stereo record, and in 1958 the major record companies followed. At first these were mainly demonstration records on which percussion bounced from left to right. In the 1960s rock bands discovered the possibilities. Producers put vocals and drums hard left or hard right, and psychedelic bands let sounds float around the room.
items.listen: Listen on headphones: what do you hear on the left, what on the right, and does anything move from one side to the other?

items.name: 45 rpm single
items.text: In 1949 RCA Victor answered the LP with a small vinyl record with a large hole, turning at 45 revolutions per minute. Each side held one song of a few minutes. The single was cheap, unbreakable and fitted jukeboxes and portable record players. That made it the product for teenagers with pocket money. In the 1950s rock 'n' roll was above all singles music: an A-side for the radio, a B-side to go with it, and a new chart every week. That is how the shape of the three-minute pop song survived.
items.listen: How quickly does the song get to the point? Count how many seconds pass before the singing starts.

items.name: Slapback echo
items.text: In his small Sun studio in Memphis, Sam Phillips used two tape recorders to create a short echo: the sound was recorded and played back again a fraction of a second later. That single quick repeat, the slapback, gave voices and guitars a spacious, bouncing sound. It became the sound of Elvis Presley's early records and of rockabilly. Soon afterwards came separate echo units with a tape loop, such as the Echoplex and the Italian Meazzi, which guitarists in indorock (the Dutch-Indonesian guitar rock of the late 1950s) and surf rock often used.
items.listen: Listen to the end of each word: can you hear the short second slap just behind the voice?

items.name: Electric guitar
items.who: George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker; Gibson (ES-150)
items.text: In a big band an acoustic guitar disappeared behind the horns. In the early 1930s, in Los Angeles, George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker built a lap steel guitar with a pickup, a magnet with a coil that turns the vibration of the string into an electric current. In 1936 Gibson released the ES-150, a hollow jazz guitar with such a pickup. In Benny Goodman's band, Charlie Christian showed that the guitar could now be a solo instrument. After the war, blues musicians in Chicago such as Muddy Waters used it to create a raw, loud urban sound.
items.listen: The guitar is up front: is it playing chords, or long melodic lines like a horn player?

tracks.title: Solo Flight
tracks.artist: Benny Goodman Orchestra met Charlie Christian

items.name: Steel guitar: lap steel and pedal steel
items.who: Joseph Kekuku; later Bud Isaacs (pedal steel)
items.text: According to tradition, the Hawaiian schoolboy Joseph Kekuku discovered around 1889 in Honolulu that he could play a guitar by sliding a piece of metal along the strings. He laid the guitar flat on his lap. A lap steel like this plays gliding notes that sound like a sighing voice. Hawaiian musicians took the instrument with them on tours of America and Europe, and in the 1930s it was given an electric pickup. In country music it became indispensable. Later, pedals were added that change the tuning of individual strings. Bud Isaacs showcased the pedal steel in 1954 on Slowly by Webb Pierce, and ever since it has wept in almost every country song.
items.listen: Listen to the gliding notes: does the guitar sound like an instrument, or more like a voice sighing?

tracks.title: Steel Guitar Rag
tracks.artist: Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys

items.name: Steelpan
items.who: Winston 'Spree' Simon, Ellie Mannette and the steel bands of Port of Spain
items.text: In Trinidad, African drums were banned from carnival in the 1880s. Revellers therefore beat on bamboo sticks, and in the 1930s also on tins, dustbins and car parts. In 1939 the first band to play only on metal paraded through Port of Spain. Boys such as Winston Spree Simon discovered that a dented piece of metal produces different notes. Around 1947 Ellie Mannette and others made pans from oil drums, which were lying around everywhere after the war. In 1951 a steel band from Trinidad presented the instrument in London. The steel band became the sound of carnival and calypso.
items.listen: You hear only metal pans: which ones play the melody, and which ones the bass and the rhythm?

items.name: Fender Precision Bass
items.text: A double bass is big, quiet and awkward to carry around. In 1951 Leo Fender released the Precision Bass: an electric bass guitar with frets, built as a solid body. Thanks to the frets a bassist could play 'precisely' in tune, hence the name. With an amplifier the bass could at last be heard above drums and guitars. In the 1960s the bass guitar became a melodic instrument. In the Motown studio in Detroit, James Jamerson played busy, syncopated bass lines that form the heart of the hits.
items.listen: Follow only the bass: does it play one note per beat, or a melody of its own with runs?

items.name: Fender Telecaster
items.text: The hollow electric guitar started to feed back when the amplifier was turned up loud. In Fullerton in 1950, radio repairman Leo Fender built a guitar from a solid slab of wood, first called the Esquire and the Broadcaster, and from 1951 the Telecaster. The neck was bolted on and the guitar was assembled in a factory from separate parts. That made it reliable and affordable. The Telecaster sounds sharp and twangy. It became the instrument of country guitarists in Bakersfield and Nashville, and later of pub rockers and punks.
items.listen: Can you hear the sharp, biting attack of the guitar, cutting through the other instruments?

items.name: Gibson Les Paul
items.who: Gibson, in collaboration with Les Paul
items.text: In 1952 Gibson answered Fender with a solid body of its own, designed together with the guitarist and inventor Les Paul. The Les Paul is heavier than a Fender, with a carved top and later double pickups, humbuckers, which hummed less. It sustains a note for a long time and sounds full and warm. In the 1960s British blues guitarists discovered that a Les Paul played through an amplifier turned right up gave a thick, singing tone. That made it the guitar of blues rock and hard rock.
items.listen: Listen to how long the guitar notes hang in the air before they die away.

items.name: Fender Stratocaster
items.text: In 1954 the Stratocaster followed: a solid body with a rounded shape, three pickups and a tremolo arm that lets you bend the pitch down and spring it back. By switching between the pickups, the same guitar can sound bright and glassy or warm and round. Buddy Holly made the Strat famous in rock 'n' roll, and Hank Marvin of The Shadows did the same in Europe. Jimi Hendrix used the tremolo arm and feedback to make notes howl and dive. The Stratocaster has since become one of the most copied guitars in the world.
items.listen: Can you hear the bright, slightly glassy sound of the guitar, and somewhere a note that bends or dips?

items.name: Amplifier and overdrive
items.who: Leo Fender (amplifiers from the 1940s), Jim Marshall (JTM45, 1962)
items.text: An amplifier is supposed to make a signal bigger without changing it. Turn it up further than intended and the peaks of the sound wave are clipped off, and the guitar sounds rough and ragged: overdrive. As early as 1958 Link Wray poked holes in his loudspeaker to get that sound. In 1962, in his music shop in Hanwell, in west London, Jim Marshall built an amplifier that let rock guitarists sound loud and distorted. Out of that sound grew hard rock and heavy metal, with the power chord as their foundation.
items.listen: Is the guitar clean or distorted? Can you hear the difference between single notes and the heavy chords?

items.name: Fuzz pedal
items.who: Glenn Snoddy and Revis Hobbs; Gibson (Maestro FZ-1)
items.text: During a Marty Robbins recording session in Nashville, one channel of the mixing desk broke down. As a result the guitar solo in Don't Worry, a hit in 1961, sounded buzzing and distorted, and the public loved it. Sound engineer Glenn Snoddy and Revis Hobbs built a circuit that created the effect on purpose. From 1962 Gibson sold it as the Maestro FZ-1 Fuzz-Tone, one of the first effects pedals. From then on any guitarist could choose between clean and dirty with a single footswitch. Fuzz became the sound of garage rock, psychedelia and, later, grunge.
items.listen: Compare the fuzz sound with an ordinary amplified guitar: does it buzz, does it crackle, does it sound like a horn?

items.name: Hammond organ and Leslie
items.text: In 1935, in Chicago, Laurens Hammond built an electric organ for churches that could not afford a pipe organ. Spinning discs, tonewheels, generate the notes, and with sliders, drawbars, you blend in the overtones. Don Leslie came up with a speaker cabinet with rotating horns that gives the organ a floating, undulating sound. Jimmy Smith made the Hammond a jazz instrument, and Booker T. Jones made it the second lead voice of soul at Stax. In British rock it sounded solemn, as in a church, or else distorted and loud.
items.listen: Can you hear the organ floating and undulating? That is the rotating Leslie speaker.

items.name: Multitrack recording
items.who: Ampex (Ross Snyder, Sel-Sync) and Les Paul
items.text: As early as around 1950, Les Paul was recording parts on top of one another by copying from one tape recorder to another. At Ampex, Ross Snyder devised a way of recording on a second track while hearing the first one back in sync. In 1957 Les Paul received the first eight-track recorder. With it a band no longer had to play at the same time: each part could be recorded separately, redone and mixed later. Pop music thus became something you build in layers, with dozens of voices and instruments that were never in a room together.
items.listen: Try counting the layers: how many voices and instruments can you hear that could not possibly have been played live at the same time?

items.name: Transistor radio
items.text: The Regency TR-1 of 1954 was the first transistor radio to go on sale in the shops. Transistors replaced the bulky radio valves, so a radio fitted in your coat pocket and ran on batteries. From then on teenagers could listen to their own music out of sight of their parents: on the beach, in the street, in their bedroom. Producers tailored their records to that tiny loudspeaker. At Motown, mixes were checked on cheap speakers, and Phil Spector built a sound that came across as full even through a minuscule radio.
items.listen: Play this song through a phone speaker: what holds up, and what drops away?

items.name: Theremin
items.text: Around 1920 the Russian physicist Lev Termen built an instrument that you play without touching it. Two antennas measure the distance to your hands: one controls the pitch, the other the volume. The sound is a gliding, singing tone reminiscent of a voice or a musical saw. Clara Rockmore played classical music on it. In Hollywood in the 1940s and 1950s the theremin became the sound of suspense, madness and flying saucers. Robert Moog started building theremins in the 1950s, before he made synthesizers. Later, rock musicians such as Jimmy Page used the theremin too.
items.listen: The tone glides from note to note without any jumps: what does that sound remind you of?

tracks.title: The Day the Earth Stood Still: Prelude / Outer Space / Radar

items.name: Vocoder
items.text: In the 1930s, at Bell Labs, Homer Dudley developed the vocoder, intended to send speech efficiently over telephone lines. The device splits a voice into frequency bands and imposes their contours on another sound, a synthesizer for example. The result is a talking machine. Wendy Carlos used the vocoder in the early 1970s in the music for A Clockwork Orange, and Kraftwerk turned it into the sound of the man-machine. After that the robot voice was heard everywhere in electro and Italo disco.
items.listen: Where do you hear the robot voice? Does it sound like a singing synthesizer or like a talking machine?

items.name: Mellotron
items.who: Leslie, Frank and Norman Bradley (Streetly Electronics), based on Harry Chamberlin's Chamberlin
items.text: Under every key of a Mellotron sits a strip of tape holding a recording of a real instrument: a violin, a flute, a choir. Press a key and that strip runs past a playback head. After about eight seconds it runs out. The instrument was built in Birmingham from 1963, modelled on the American Chamberlin. The strings and choirs sound not quite real and waver slightly, and that is exactly what became a sound of its own. The Mellotron is a forerunner of the sampler and became the sound of prog rock.
items.listen: Do the strings or choirs sound like a real orchestra? Notice how the notes waver slightly.

items.name: Wall of Sound
items.text: At Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles, producer Phil Spector had several guitarists, pianists and drummers play the same part at the same time, and sent the sound through an echo chamber. In this way all the instruments melted together into one thick wall of sound, the Wall of Sound. It was designed to sound overwhelming even from a small radio. Spector treated the studio not as a place to capture a band, but as an instrument in its own right. That is how girl groups such as The Ronettes got their grand sound, and later Bruce Springsteen built on it.
items.listen: Try to pick out individual instruments. Can you, or do you mainly hear one big mass?

items.name: Compact cassette
items.text: Lou Ottens's team at Philips in Hasselt developed a small plastic box containing magnetic tape, which was presented in 1963. Philips licensed the format freely to other manufacturers, and the cassette became a worldwide standard. From then on anyone could record music at home, copy it and make their own mixtape. After the Sony Walkman of 1979, you could take that music out onto the street as well. Bands released their first demos on cassette, and in Algeria raï spread mainly through cheap cassettes, bypassing the radio.
items.listen: This song spread through copies and tapes: what does the sound tell you about who it was meant for?

items.name: Moog synthesizer
items.text: From 1964, in Trumansburg, Robert Moog built synthesizers from separate modules that you connected with cables. An oscillator makes a tone, a filter removes overtones from it, and an envelope determines how the tone starts and fades away. The modules control one another with electrical voltage. In 1968 Wendy Carlos showed what the instrument could do with Switched-On Bach, and the album was a huge success. After that, rock bands used the Moog for solos and new tone colours. The characteristic sound lies mainly in the filter, which lets a tone 'open up'.
items.listen: Can you hear a tone that opens up from dull to bright? That is the Moog's filter.

items.name: 8-track
items.who: Bill Lear (Lear Jet), with Ford and Motorola
items.text: In 1964 aircraft maker Bill Lear designed the Stereo 8: a cartridge with an endless loop of magnetic tape and eight tracks, four stereo programmes side by side. Ford offered the player in its cars from the 1966 models onwards, and for the first time you chose for yourself what you heard on the road. In the United States the 8-track was hugely popular in the 1970s, especially in the car. Because an album was divided over four programmes, a click sometimes sounded in the middle of a song, after which the song carried on. Around 1980 the compact cassette pushed the format aside.
items.listen: In the 1970s you heard this through the car speakers: why does this music work so well on the motorway?

items.name: Talk box
items.who: Bob Heil; later Peter Frampton and Roger Troutman (Zapp)
items.text: A talkbox makes a guitar talk. A speaker blows the sound through a thin plastic tube into the musician's mouth, where lips and tongue shape it into vowels, and a microphone picks up the result. The idea had been around since the late 1930s, but the devices were too quiet for a rock stage. In 1973 sound engineer Bob Heil of Marissa, Illinois built a powerful version for Joe Walsh, who used it on Rocky Mountain Way. Peter Frampton turned it into a crowd-pleaser. In funk, Roger Troutman of Zapp sent a synthesizer singing through the talkbox, and that sound returned in G-funk.
items.listen: Can you hear where the guitar stops and the voice begins? Which words or vowels can you make out?

items.name: Fender Rhodes
items.text: Harold Rhodes developed an electric piano without strings. A small hammer strikes a thin metal rod, and a pickup turns that vibration into an electrical signal, just as on a guitar. After a bass version in 1959, the full Fender Rhodes came onto the market in 1965. Its sound is warm and softly bell-like, and it starts to growl when you play harder. In the late sixties Miles Davis had his pianists play the Rhodes, and the instrument became a fixture of jazz rock and soul, and later of neo-soul.
items.listen: Listen to the keyboard part: can you hear the soft, bell-like tone, and the growl when the keys are struck hard?

tracks.title: You Are the Sunshine of My Life

items.name: The studio as instrument
items.who: The Beatles with George Martin and the EMI engineers; Brian Wilson in Los Angeles
items.text: In 1966 the Beatles stopped touring and began working mainly in the studio. With producer George Martin and EMI's engineers they used tape loops, tape played backwards, varied tape speeds and ADT, a trick in which a second tape recorder automatically doubles a voice. In Los Angeles, Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys built Pet Sounds with session musicians. A record was no longer a document of a performance, but a work that could only exist in the studio. Psychedelic rock and art rock grew out of this.
items.listen: Which sounds on this recording could no band play live on a stage?

items.name: Wah-wah pedal
items.who: Brad Plunkett (Warwick Electronics / Thomas Organ Company)
items.text: In 1966 Brad Plunkett at the Thomas Organ Company developed a pedal with a filter that you open and close with your foot. It makes the guitar sound as if it is saying 'wa-wa', like a trumpet with a mute. The pedal was sold under the Vox and Cry Baby brands. Jimi Hendrix turned it into a talking, wailing voice. In the early seventies, funk and soul guitarists played the wah rhythmically instead, and so it became the sound of blaxploitation films such as Shaft.
items.listen: Can you hear the guitar 'talking'? Notice how the sound opens and closes in time with the rhythm.

items.name: Minimoog
items.who: R.A. Moog Inc. (Robert Moog, Bill Hemsath, Jim Scott, Chad Hunt)
items.text: The big modular Moog was a cabinet full of cables, made for a studio. In 1970 came the Minimoog: a portable synthesizer with the most important parts built in, no patch cords needed. You could put it on a stage next to the organ, and the synthesizer became an ordinary band instrument. The Minimoog plays one note at a time and is famous for its fat bass lines and sharp lead sounds. Bernie Worrell used it to play the bass in Parliament's funk, Kraftwerk used it on Autobahn, and Gary Numan brought it into synthpop.
items.listen: Look for the deep, round synth bass or the bright synth melody: which one is the Minimoog playing?

items.name: Rhythm machine
items.text: In 1959 the organ maker Wurlitzer released the Side Man, a cabinet with a rotating disc that triggered electronic drum sounds in the rhythm of a waltz, a rumba or a foxtrot. It was meant for organists in bars and restaurants, who then no longer had to pay a drummer. Later, electronic organs came with such rhythms built in. In 1971 Sly Stone made a Maestro Rhythm King the foundation of his album There's a Riot Goin' On. The stiff, dry rhythm suddenly sounded weary and menacing. Timmy Thomas set an organ with built-in rhythms to bossa nova, and Shuggie Otis jammed for hours along with his own rhythm machine.
items.listen: The rhythm comes from a machine: does it sound like a drummer, or can you hear how mechanical it is?

items.name: Technics SL-1200 and scratching
items.who: Matsushita (Technics, team led by Shuichi Obata); DJs in the Bronx
items.text: In 1972 Matsushita released the SL-1200 under the Technics name, a direct-drive turntable. Its motor is strong and holds its speed, even when you stop the record with your hand or pull it back. DJs in the Bronx used two turntables to repeat the drum break of a funk record endlessly. Moving the record rhythmically back and forth gave rise to scratching, which turned the turntable into an instrument. The SL-1200 became the standard in hip hop and club DJ booths all over the world.
items.listen: Can you hear the scraping scratch sound? That is a DJ moving a record back and forth by hand.

tracks.title: The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel

items.name: The mixing desk as instrument (dub)
items.text: In Kingston, producers made an instrumental version without vocals for the B-side of their singles. Engineer King Tubby went further: in his small studio he dropped instruments in and out on the mixing desk, added long echo and reverb, and filtered the sound. In this way an existing recording was turned into a new track: dub. The mixing desk was his instrument. Ideas from dub, such as space, a heavy bass and the remix, returned in hip hop, jungle, trip hop and dubstep.
items.listen: Notice what drops out and comes back: which instrument disappears into the echo, and when?

items.name: Sound system
items.who: Tom the Great Sebastian, Duke Reid, Coxsone Dodd and others
items.text: From the fifties onwards, sound systems played in the poor neighbourhoods of Kingston: mobile discos with home-built amplifiers and enormous speaker cabinets. At first they played American rhythm and blues, later Jamaica's own records. Owners such as Duke Reid and Coxsone Dodd began recording records themselves, so as to have something their rivals did not. The deejay talked and toasted over the music, a forerunner of rap. DJ Kool Herc took that custom with him to the Bronx, where it grew into hip hop.
items.listen: The deejay talks and shouts over an existing record: can you hear how the voice becomes an instrument?

items.name: Fairlight CMI
items.text: In 1979 the Australians Peter Vogel and Kim Ryrie released the Fairlight CMI, a computer with a keyboard and a light pen. It could record a real sound digitally and put it under the keys, at any pitch: a sampler. The idea behind the Mellotron now worked without tapes, with any sound you could record. The Fairlight was so expensive that only stars and big studios could afford one. Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush and producer Trevor Horn built entire records with it.
items.listen: Can you hear sounds that start out as real instruments or noises, but repeat with unnatural precision?

tracks.title: Running Up That Hill (A Deal With God)

items.name: Sequential Prophet-5
items.who: Dave Smith and John Bowen (Sequential Circuits)
items.text: The Minimoog could only play one note at a time. Dave Smith and John Bowen of Sequential Circuits in San Jose built a synthesizer that plays five notes at once, so chords as well. This is called polyphonic. What was really new was the memory: a small computer stored all the settings of a sound, so that you could switch sounds at the press of a button, even on stage. Smith showed the Prophet-5 in January 1978 at the NAMM trade show in California. It became a sound of new wave and synthpop, from The Cars and Japan to Talking Heads, and later of Michael Jackson and Madonna.
items.listen: Listen to the keyboards: is the synthesizer playing single melodies or full chords, and how does the sound change?

tracks.title: This Must Be the Place (Naive Melody)

items.name: Sony Walkman
items.who: Sony (Nobutoshi Kihara, Kozo Ohsone; idea by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita)
items.text: Sony co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted to listen to music on long flights. For him, engineers in Tokyo built a small cassette player with no speaker and no record button, and a pair of lightweight headphones. On 1 July 1979 the Walkman went on sale in Japan. Many people inside Sony had their doubts: who wants a cassette player that cannot record? It became a worldwide success. Music became something personal, a soundtrack to your own walk or bus ride. The city became the backdrop to your music. Young people played their home-made tapes on it, full of new wave, postpunk and synthpop.
items.listen: Imagine hearing this on headphones as you walk through the city: what does the music do to what you see?

items.name: TASCAM Portastudio
items.text: In the seventies a multitrack studio was expensive and large. In September 1979 TEAC, under its TASCAM brand, unveiled the 144 Portastudio: a mixing desk and a recorder for ordinary cassettes in a single box. You could record four tracks separately and layer them on top of each other, for 899 dollars. From then on, musicians made their demos at home. On 3 January 1982 Bruce Springsteen recorded songs on a Portastudio in his bedroom in Colts Neck. Those recordings were released almost untouched as the album Nebraska. In the nineties Guided by Voices and Elliott Smith made whole albums on four-track recorders. That raw home sound is called lo-fi.
items.listen: Can you hear the hiss and the room? What does that home-recorded sound add to the song?

items.name: Linn LM-1
items.text: In 1980 Roger Linn released the LM-1, the first drum machine to use digital recordings of real drums instead of electronically imitated sounds. You programmed a pattern and the machine played it back tightly and endlessly, with a built-in option to give the rhythm a little swing. The cheaper LinnDrum followed in 1982. These machines can be heard on countless hits of the eighties, from The Human League and Michael Jackson to Prince, who often used the drums tuned and processed in unusual ways.
items.listen: Do the drums sound like a drummer or like a machine? Notice how even every beat is.

items.name: Gated reverb
items.who: Hugh Padgham, Steve Lillywhite, Phil Collins and Peter Gabriel
items.text: Gated reverb means reverb with a gate. In 1979 Peter Gabriel was recording his third solo album at the Townhouse Studios in London, with Phil Collins on drums. The new mixing desk had a microphone in the recording room for talking to the musicians. It made quiet sounds as loud as loud ones, and so blew up every drum hit and the room's reverb. Engineer Hugh Padgham put a gate on it that cuts the sound off abruptly. Every hit sounded enormous, followed by sudden silence. Gabriel built Intruder around that sound, and Collins used it in In the Air Tonight. It became the drum sound of the eighties.
items.listen: Listen to the drums: how big does a hit sound, and how quickly does the reverb vanish afterwards?

items.name: Roland TR-808
items.text: The Roland TR-808 came onto the market in 1980 as an aid for making demos. It uses no recordings of real drums: every sound is generated electronically. Musicians thought it sounded fake, and Roland stopped making it after a few years. Second-hand it became cheap, and young producers discovered its bass drum, which rings out long and low, a sub-bass you feel more than hear. The 808 became the foundation of electro, Miami bass and trap, and in hip hop '808' now simply means a deep, long bass.
items.listen: Listen to the bass drum: is it a short thud, or a long, low tone that slowly fades away?

items.name: Roland TB-303
items.text: The TB-303 Bass Line was meant for guitarists who practised alone and missed having a bass player. The little box has one oscillator, a filter and a sequencer in which you program a bass line note by note, with accents and sliding notes. It did not sound like a bass guitar and flopped; in 1984 it went out of production. In Chicago, producers discovered that you could turn the cutoff and resonance knobs while it was playing. The same bass line then starts to squeal, quack and wail. That sound was given the name acid.
items.listen: The notes stay almost the same, but the sound keeps changing: can you hear the filter opening and closing?

tracks.title: Higher State of Consciousness (Tweekin Acid Funk Mix)

items.name: MTV and the music video
items.text: On 1 August 1981 MTV launched in the United States, a television channel that broadcast music videos all day long. The first video was Video Killed the Radio Star by The Buggles. From then on a pop star also had to look good on screen, with clothes, hair and a story. British synthpop and New Romantic groups, who were already working with images, conquered the American charts this way. In its first years MTV played almost nothing but white rock; that only changed when Michael Jackson's videos made it onto the channel.
items.listen: This song became big through its music video: what images does it conjure up in your head?

items.name: Compact disc (CD)
items.text: Philips and Sony jointly developed the compact disc, which came onto the market in 1982. Music is stored on it as digital code: 44,100 measurements per second per channel, read by a laser. A CD has no hiss and does not wear out, and it holds over an hour of music. In the nineties the CD became the standard and the industry earned more than ever, partly because people bought their old records again. But a digital copy is exactly the same as the original. With a CD burner and a computer, the way to free copying lay open.
items.listen: Listen to the silences and the quiet passages: can you hear hiss or clicks, as you would on a vinyl record or cassette?

items.name: Yamaha DX7
items.who: Yamaha, based on the FM synthesis of John Chowning (Stanford)
items.text: The Yamaha DX7 of 1983 did not work with filters, but with FM synthesis: one wave makes the frequency of another go up and down very rapidly. The principle came from John Chowning of Stanford University. The sound is bright, glassy and metallic, good for electric pianos, bells and punchy basses. The DX7 was affordable and reliable and became one of the best-selling synthesizers ever. Because programming it was difficult, many musicians used the factory sounds, such as the electric piano and the slap bass. Those defined the sound of the eighties.
items.listen: Look for the bright, slightly metallic synth sound or the punchy synth bass: that is what FM sounds like.

tracks.title: Take My Breath Away (Love Theme from Top Gun)

items.name: MIDI
items.text: Until 1983, synthesizers from different makers could not talk to each other. Dave Smith of Sequential and Ikutaro Kakehashi of Roland proposed a shared standard, MIDI, which was first demonstrated in January 1983 at the NAMM music trade show in Anaheim. Through MIDI, instruments and computers tell each other which note is sounding, how loud and for how long. With one keyboard you could play several synthesizers, or have a computer play everything back. This made home studios with an Atari computer and a sampler affordable. Every DAW still works with MIDI.
items.listen: Everything in this track runs tightly together: which parts would a computer be controlling here?

items.name: Roland TR-909
items.text: The TR-909 of 1983 was the successor to the 808. The bass drum, snare and toms are still generated electronically, but the cymbals and hi-hats are digital recordings. The machine also had MIDI. The 909 sold poorly too and became cheap second-hand. Producers in Chicago and Detroit used its solid, dry bass drum on every beat with the hissing open hi-hat in between. That pattern became the foundation of house and techno, and after that of almost all European dance music.
items.listen: Count along with the bass drum on every beat, and listen to the hi-hat hissing in between each time.

items.name: Beat sampler (SP-1200, MPC)
items.who: E-mu Systems (SP-1200); Akai with Roger Linn (MPC60, 1988)
items.text: With the E-mu SP-1200 of 1987 and the Akai MPC60 of 1988, a producer could record a snippet of a record, chop it into pieces and assign them to pads. By tapping the pads you play the pieces like a drum kit made of samples, and a built-in sequencer arranges them into a pattern. In this way hip hop became a collage of drums, horns and bass lines from old records. The short sampling time and slightly grainy sound of the SP-1200 became a sound in their own right. J Dilla played the pads in by hand, without quantize, which gives his beats a loose swing.
items.listen: Which snippets come from old records? Can you hear the grain and the repetition of a sample?

tracks.title: Building Steam with a Grain of Salt

items.name: Breakbeat sampling (the Amen break)
items.who: Producers in the British rave and jungle scene
items.text: In 1969 drummer Gregory Coleman played a drum solo lasting a few seconds on Amen, Brother by The Winstons. Hip hop producers sampled that break in the late eighties. In the early nineties, producers in London went further: they sped up the Amen break and other breaks to well over 160 beats per minute and used samplers to chop them into tiny pieces, which they put in new orders. Underneath they laid heavy bass lines taken from dub. This gave rise to jungle, and out of that came drum and bass.
items.listen: Do you recognise the same drum break at a different tempo? Listen to how the pieces have been cut into a new order.

items.name: Pro Tools and the DAW
items.text: In 1991 Digidesign released Pro Tools, a system that let you record and edit multiple tracks on an Apple computer without tape. A program like this is called a digital audio workstation, or DAW. In 1999 Livin' la Vida Loca by Ricky Martin became the first number 1 hit to be recorded and mixed entirely in Pro Tools. Later, programs such as Logic, Cubase, FL Studio and Ableton Live turned every laptop into a studio. A bedroom producer can now make a complete record at home, with plug-ins that imitate old synthesizers and drum machines.
items.listen: This track was made in the computer: can you hear how tightly edited it is, with everything precisely in place?

items.name: FL Studio (FruityLoops)
items.text: At Image-Line, a software company in Ghent, nineteen-year-old Didier Dambrin wrote a simple program for making drum rhythms. FruityLoops came out at the start of 1998: a grid of boxes in which you click with the mouse where a beat should fall. It grew into a complete studio and has been called FL Studio since 2003. There was a free trial version, and a generation of bedroom producers learned to make beats with it. Soulja Boy made Crank That with that trial version, the Dutch producer Martin Garrix worked on Animals in it, and YoungKio used it to build the beat of Old Town Road, which he sold online for a few dozen dollars.
items.listen: These beats were made on a home computer: can you hear the pattern that repeats over and over?

items.name: Ableton Live
items.who: Gerhard Behles, Robert Henke and Bernd Roggendorf
items.text: Gerhard Behles and Robert Henke made techno in Berlin as Monolake. They wrote their own software so they could perform live with a computer. Together with Bernd Roggendorf they developed that idea into Ableton Live, which came out in 2001. Other programs had been made for the studio; Live was made above all for the stage. You trigger separate pieces of music, loops, and they always stay in time. The program also stretches or squeezes recordings until they fit the tempo. DJs and producers began using it both to perform and to compose. Skrillex made most of his EP Bangarang on tour in 2011, with Live on a laptop.
items.listen: Listen to the repeated pieces: how are separate loops stacked on top of each other and then taken away again?

items.name: Auto-Tune
items.text: Andy Hildebrand used mathematics from the oil industry to measure the pitch of a voice. His software Auto-Tune, released in 1997, quietly nudges out-of-tune notes to the right pitch. On Believe by Cher, the producers set the correction speed to zero. As a result the voice jumped from note to note with no transition, with an audible little kink. What was meant to be inaudible became an effect. T-Pain made it his trademark, and in trap, Afrobeats and hyperpop Auto-Tune became an ordinary part of the voice.
items.listen: Listen to the long notes: does the voice glide naturally, or does it jump from note to note with a little kink?

items.name: MP3 and Napster
items.who: Fraunhofer-Institut (Karlheinz Brandenburg); Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker
items.text: At the Fraunhofer-Institut in Erlangen, Karlheinz Brandenburg and his colleagues, among others, developed the mp3: a file format that leaves out what the ear can barely hear. This makes a song roughly ten times smaller. In June 1999 student Shawn Fanning in Boston, together with Sean Parker, released Napster, a program that let millions of people download mp3s for free from each other's computers. Metallica and the record companies went to court, and in 2001 Napster went offline. The sharing carried on, and CD sales never recovered.
items.listen: This song played a part in the history of the mp3 and Napster. Read the explanation and think about why it was this song in particular.

items.name: iPod and the iTunes Store
items.text: In October 2001 Apple unveiled the iPod: a small player with a hard drive and a scroll wheel, putting 'a thousand songs in your pocket'. In April 2003 the iTunes Store opened, where you could legally download songs for 99 cents each. From then on you bought a single song instead of a whole album, and the single returned as a file. Apple's adverts, with silhouettes dancing to music by bands such as Jet and Feist, themselves became a way of making a hit.
items.listen: This song was used in an iPod advert: why does it suit the image of someone dancing with earbuds in?

tracks.title: Are You Gonna Be My Girl

items.name: YouTube
items.who: Chad Hurley, Steve Chen and Jawed Karim
items.text: YouTube started in 2005 as a website where anyone could share videos. Within a few years it was where the music video had moved to, and for many young people the main way of listening to music. Artists could find an audience without a record company: Justin Bieber was discovered through clips on YouTube. Chicago drill rappers such as Chief Keef became known in 2012 through home-made videos. Gangnam Style by PSY was the first video to be viewed more than a billion times, and it brought K-pop to worldwide attention.
items.listen: This song became big through a video: what about its sound or its hook makes it so shareable?

items.name: SoundCloud
items.text: SoundCloud was founded in 2007 by the Swedes Alexander Ljung and Eric Wahlforss and made its home in Berlin. On the platform anyone can upload their own tracks for free, and listeners can comment at an exact moment in a song. Around 2015 a new rap scene grew up there, SoundCloud rap: young artists recording at home, with distorted 808s, short songs and lots of Auto-Tune. Hyperpop also found its first audience there. A track could go viral there without a label or radio.
items.listen: Can you hear that this was made at home? Notice the distorted bass and how short and direct the song is.

items.name: Streaming (Spotify)
items.text: In October 2008 Spotify launched in Stockholm. You no longer bought songs, but paid for access to the entire catalogue, or listened for free with adverts. The playlist took over the role of the album, and an algorithm helps decide what you hear. A stream only counts after thirty seconds, and that changed the shape of pop songs: shorter intros, the hook early on, shorter songs. Artists are paid per stream. At the same time, music from Lagos or Johannesburg could reach a worldwide audience through playlists.
items.listen: How quickly does the hook arrive? Count the seconds until you know what the song is about.

items.name: TikTok
items.text: TikTok, the short-video app from the Chinese company ByteDance, broke through worldwide in 2018. Users pick a sound clip and make a video to go with it. A few seconds of a song can be shared millions of times this way, in videos made by the users themselves. In 2019 Old Town Road by Lil Nas X became a worldwide hit in this way. Since then record companies have been looking for songs with a moment that works in a short video, and artists sometimes release a snippet first to see whether it catches on.
items.listen: Which snippet of this song would you choose for a fifteen-second video?
